<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD's top-level scope contains only variable assignments, array definitions, and a conditional that appends to makedepends — all standard packaging constructs. There is no explicit pkgver() function; the pkgver variable is a static string interpolation of predefined variables. The source array (after the second assignment overwrites the first) contains a single git+https entry pointing to the project's own upstream repository (github.com/ruffle-rs/ruffle.git), which is expected for this package. No top-level code performs network requests, downloads and executes payloads, exfiltrates data, or manipulates files outside the normal source-fetching context. The commands `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` will clone the declared git source and parse the PKGBUILD without executing prepare(), build(), or package(). No genuinely malicious behavior is present in the code paths that execute during these commands.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>
No malicious code in top-level scope or pkgver; source is from project upstream.
</summary>
</security_assessment>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD appears to be a legitimate nightly build of Ruffle (a Flash Player emulator written in Rust). The source is correctly specified as the official GitHub repository (ruffle-rs/ruffle) with a dynamic tag referencing the channel and date. The build process follows standard Rust/AUR conventions using cargo build with appropriate targets (host-tuple and wasm32-unknown-unknown). Network activity is confined to the project's own upstream (GitHub) and legitimate distribution channels (Google Cloud for Chrome extension). The installation of the Firefox extension uses a placeholder ID pattern (_FIREFOX_EXTENSION_ID) which is typical for development builds and does not indicate any malicious intent. All operations are within the scope of the application itself—building the project, running tests, and installing binaries and resources into the package directory. There are no signs of supply chain compromise, unauthorized code injection, or attempts to exfiltrate data or execute malicious code.
</details>

The source URLs point to the official Ruffle upstream repository (`ruffle-rs/ruffle`), which is expected and standard for an AUR package. No obfuscated code, no unexpected network destinations, no eval or base64 operations at the top level.
</details>
